title: Part I Protheoria: Who rejected the Formula of Concord — Ludwig's five charges; Ursinus
pass_a_gloss: Qui Formulam Concord. improbat: confessed that many Electors/Princes/Theologians across Lutheran Germany protested this temerity — and the King of the Danes — especially Elector Palatine Ludwig (as lately noted). Alting Hist. MS. Palatina: Ludwig reprehended five things in Bergen Formula — (1) restricted AC to first Exemplar offered Caesar 1530, excluding editions with any change/variation for greater evidence; (2) after naming Flaccians/Osiandrists/Antinomians left other names (e.g. Synergists) with Melanchthon's sentence less candidly explained; (3) subjected Supper/Presence doctrine to Ubiquity — which Luther neither approved nor thought fit for this Supper Controv.; (4) imported many phrases & abstract terms outside/beyond Scripture, not serving Church edification; (5) condemned Zwinglians & Calvinists with hard voice — not without appearance of Pontifical tyranny — even unheard, less convicted of error. Yet Princes' facility on one side + those Theologians' industry on the other won: Prefation by Schmidlin & Chemnitz (buskins & captious turns, as judged) induced subscription. Soon after, Apology of the Book composed at Erfurt, Chemnitz as standard-bearer, to be censured through Academies/Churches, published 1583. Meanwhile in the Palatinate Zacharias Ursinus ordered by Johann Casimir (Ludwig Elector's brother) to give a refutation of the Book — among the Neustadt Acts — than which Alting in that MS History (once usable to us at Heidelberg) praises nothing fuller, more accurate, or more learned ever written/published against these Lutherans.
pass_b_english: It is confessed that Electors, Princes, and very many Theologians throughout Lutheran Germany protested against this temerity — and the King of the Danes himself — especially Elector Ludwig of the Palatinate, as was lately noted. And Heinrich Alting notes him in the manuscript Palatine History as having reprehended five things in that Bergen Formula: (1) That it had restricted the Augsburg Confession to the first Exemplar offered to the Emperor in 1530, excluding Editions in which some change or variation had entered for the sake of greater evidence. (2) That after introducing the names of Flaccians, Osiandrists, and Antinomians, they had left other names — such as that of the Synergists — with Melanchthon's sentence less candidly explained. (3) That to the doctrine of the Lord's Supper and of Christ's Presence in that same Supper they had subjected the doctrine of Ubiquity, which Luther had neither approved nor thought fit to be employed in this Controversy concerning the Supper. (4) That they had brought into that Formula many phrases and abstract terms outside and beyond Scripture, and not serving the edification of the Church. (5) That they condemned Zwinglians and Calvinists — not without the appearance of Pontifical tyranny — using this hard voice, even those not heard, and still less convicted of error.

Yet at length the facility of the Princes on that side, and the industry employed by those Theologians on this, won out — by which, with a Prefation written by Schmidlin and Chemnitz, consisting of tragic buskins and captious turns (so it was judged), they induced those men to subscribe. And not long afterward they composed an Apology of this Book at Erfurt, with Martin Chemnitz as standard-bearer, to be censured through the Academies and Churches, and to be published in 1583. Meanwhile among the Palatines Zacharias Ursinus was ordered by Johann Casimir, brother of Elector Ludwig, to give a refutation of the Book, which is among the Neustadt Acts — and than which, the praised Alting says in that manuscript History which we were once permitted to use at Heidelberg, nothing fuller, nothing more accurate, nothing more learned was ever written and published against these Lutherans.
source_text: Reclamasse adversus hanc temeritatem Electores, Principes, Theologos per Germaniam Lutheranam plurimos, in confesso est, ipsumque Danorum Regem, in specie Electorem Palatinum Ludovicum, ut nuper observatum. Et hunc in Hist. MS. Palatina notat H. Altingius, quinque reprehendisse in ea Bergensi Formula; 1. Quod Augustanam Confessionem restrinxisset ad primum Exemplar, oblatum Caesari A. 1530, exclusis Editionibus, in quibus mutatio seu variatio aliqua accesserat, majoris evidentiae causa. 2. Quod inductis nominibus Flaccianorum, Osiandristarum, Antinomorum, reliquissent alia, uti Synergistarum nomen, minus candide explicata sententia Melanchthonis. 3. Quod doctrinae de Coena Domini & Praesentia Christi in eadem Coena, subjecissent doctrinam de Ubiquitate, quam nec probasset Lutherus, nec putasset adhibendam in hac de Coena Controversia. 4. Quod phrases multas, & abstractivas voces, extra & praeter Scripturam, nec aedificationi Ecclesiae inservientes, in eam Formulam intulissent. 5. Quod Zwinglianos & Calvinianos, non sine specie tyrannidis Pontificiae, damnarent, hac dura voce adhibita, etiam non auditos, minus convictos errore. Sed vicit tandem illinc facilitas Principum, hinc adhibita a Theologis istis industria, qua, Praefatione scripta a Schmidlino & Chemnitio, cothurnis constante & captionibus, (sic judicatum) ad subscribendum illos induxerunt. Nec diu post Apologiam hujus Libri Erfordiae concinnarunt, antesignano M. Chemnitio, censendam per Academias Ecclesiasque, & edendam A. 1583. Dum in Palatinis Zach. Ursinus jussus est a Joh. Casimiro, Fratre Ludovici Elect. dare refutationem Libri, quae inter Acta Neostadiana est, & qua nihil plenius, nihil accuratius, nihil doctius, contra hos Lutheranos, unquam Scriptum editumque esse, laudatus Altingius in MS. ea Historia, quam Heidelbergae olim usurpare nobis licuit.
